# Root Cause

Find why a failure happened by asking why until the answer stops changing. Then name the control that would have refused it.

## Rules

- **Analyse a signal, not one occurrence.** A change made in response to normal variation increases the variation.
- **Every link cites an observation.** A link that you reasoned to is where the chain becomes a story.
- **Stop at a cause you control.** A vendor decision or "the model was wrong" gives you nothing to build a control against.
- **Never stop on a person.** "Someone forgot" means the chain stopped early. Ask what let the mistake reach a commit.
- **Record the branch you did not take.** Two analysts reach different causes from the same incident.
- **Deliver a control, not advice.** "Be careful" and "add a note" prevent nothing.

## 1. Check that it is a signal

A signal is a point beyond three standard deviations, or a run or a trend inside the limits. The cheaper test is this question: has this shape happened before? Query the ledger before you analyse:

```sh
jq -r 'select(.kind=="created")|.payload.title // empty' .basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl \
  | rg -i '<the shape>'
rg -c '<the marker>' .basicly/usage/run-records.json
```

A record title is only on its `created` event. A query over every event returns nothing, and nothing reads as "no prior". Confirm that the first stage of the pipeline prints titles before you believe a zero.

One occurrence with no prior: record it and stop.

## 2. Ask why

Ask why until the answer stops changing. Each link cites a `file:line`, a command and its output, a ledger row or a recorded verdict. When the next why leaves this repository, go back one link and build the control there.

At each link where a second answer was available, name it and say why you took the other one.

## 3. Test the chain

- **Per cause: would the removal of this cause block this path?** If the failure still reaches the same end, the cause is a condition you noticed. Continue the chain.
- **For the set: would the removal of all retained causes block the observed failure?** If a route stays open, a link is missing. That link is the one that needs the control.

A second person can run these two tests against your chain without a new derivation.

## 4. Output

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Control | A check, a gate, a schema field or a refusal that would have refused this defect |
| Tier | `control` (fails a gate), `warning` (reports and continues) or `documentation` (a person must read it). Record a `documentation` tier as a downgrade, with the reason that no stronger control was available |
| Covers | The whole class of defects, not this one instance. A control for one incident is a patch |
| Branch not taken | One line |

Deliver the control as a diff against catalog YAML: a fragment, a skill, a hook or a schema field. A person approves it before it lands. `basicly catalog lint` and the projection checks limit what they approve.

## Example

```text
Signal      3 of 5 lanes failed to land on one shared anchor, twice in one pass
Why 1       the rebase conflicted            (the merge result names the conflict)
Why 2       two lanes appended at one anchor (both scope globs name basicly.toml)
Why 3       decompose grouped the work by scope-glob overlap, which is file adjacency
Why 4       scope globs are the only structure the decomposer can see
STOP        we control that

Branch not taken: "generate the anchors". Real, but it fixes three files, not the
slicing rule that keeps producing collisions.

Control     a plan-gate refusal when two children declare an overlapping anchor
Tier        control
Covers      every decomposition that slices by file adjacency
```
